To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

UK pension fund managers opportunistically inflated their reported expected rates of return on pension fund assets during a period of major changes to accounting standards, and that this opportunistic behaviour was stronger during the transitional adoption of a new accounting standard.

UK firms with tighter debt covenants and those with lower leverage reported higher expected rates of return on pension investments during an extended period in which pension accounting rules were changing.

UK firms opportunistically reported ERRs to manage their balance sheet leverage during the period of major changes to the pension reporting regime (1998–2012), with the opportunistic reporting behaviour increasing during the transitional period of FRS 19 adoption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
whether UK pension managers behaved opportunististically when determining the ERRs during the period of major changes to pension accounting rules (FRS 17).
the determinants of the expected rate of returns on pension assets, and the role of ERRs in the management of pension costs and leverage.
whether UK firms opportunistically determined their ERRs during a period of major pension accounting changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the UK firms with tightening financial covenants have a strong incentive to manage their pension liabilities and they have been using their pension accounting flexibility to manage the reported pension costs.
the ERRs were used as a tool to manage balance sheet debt covenants and that the use of this tool was strengthened when the FRS 16 to FRS 17 transition occurred.
the ERR is a useful indicator of the expected rate of future returns, and that the ERR is not a measure of the expected rate at which pension assets grow.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the contracting hypothesis is supported, that the cost of contracting is higher during the FRS17 transitional adoption period and that firms used the ERRs jointly with salary growth to manage leverage.

the contracting incentive to overstate ERRs is stronger in the presence of debt covenant tightening, and the incentive to manage balance sheet debt is stronger during the FASB's transitional adoption period.
the UK's FRS 17 pension accounting standard was successful in its objective of increasing transparency in the reporting of pension costs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accounting for pension costs is an area of accounting where the IASB should continue to monitor the effects of changes in accounting rules.

pension accounting rules can have a significant impact on the reliability of reported financial statements, and that the reliability of reported information can be enhanced when accounting standards require more precise and consistent reporting of pension costs.
the ERRs are not a good indicator of future pension liabilities, and that pension accounting rules should be revised to improve the reliability of reported information.
